chapter.name: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
chapter.blurb: Doubling and halving a square using its diagonal; the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle and the square root of 2; combining two different squares to derive a squared + b squared = c squared; Baudhayana (Pythagorean) triples, primitive and scaled, and Fermat's Last Theorem as a historical aside; and applications to word problems, rhombi, rectangles and equilateral triangles.

scope_in.item: Doubling a square by constructing a new square on its diagonal, and why this works (the original square's two triangles fit inside the new square's four congruent triangles)
Halving a square by folding through the midpoints of its sides (or by reversing the doubling construction), producing a tilted inner square of half the area
The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle: deriving c squared = 2 times a squared from the doubling construction, and using it to find c given a, or a given c

Decimal bounds for the square root of 2 (between 1 and 2, and more closely between 1.414 and 1.415) found by successive squaring, and the argument that the square root of 2 cannot be a terminating decimal or a fraction m/n

Combining two different-sized squares into one larger square using Baudhayana's rectangle-and-diagonal construction, leading to the general theorem a squared + b squared = c squared for any right-angled triangle

Baudhayana (Pythagorean) triples: the definition a squared + b squared = c squared for positive integers, scaling a triple by a positive integer k, primitive triples, and generating triples from consecutive odd squares
Fermat's Last Theorem as a historical extension of Baudhayana triples to higher powers, stated without proof, and its proof by Andrew Wiles in 1994

Applying a squared + b squared = c squared to word problems (such as the Lilavati lotus-in-the-lake problem) and to geometric figures: the diagonal of a square or rectangle, the side of a rhombus from its diagonals, the hypotenuse as the longest side of a right triangle, integer-sided rectangles, and the area of an equilateral triangle via its altitude

scope_out.item: A general proof of the Pythagoras theorem using similar triangles or the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse
scope_out.reason: This book proves the theorem only through Baudhayana's square-combining dissection; the similar-triangles proof is not used here

scope_out.item: Trigonometric ratios such as sine, cosine and tangent
scope_out.reason: Not introduced anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: The distance formula between two points on a coordinate plane
scope_out.reason: Coordinates are not used in this chapter; the grid and rhombus questions are solved by direct right-triangle reasoning, not a named formula

scope_out.item: A proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, or details of Andrew Wiles's method
scope_out.reason: The chapter presents the theorem and its history as a story; it explicitly says no one could find Fermat's own proof

scope_out.item: Irrationality proofs for square roots other than the square root of 2, such as the square root of 3 or the square root of 5
scope_out.reason: The chapter proves only the square root of 2 is irrational, using a prime-factorisation argument specific to the number 2

scope_out.item: Three-dimensional applications such as the space diagonal of a cuboid
scope_out.reason: This chapter stays with plane figures; solids are not discussed

concepts.name: Doubling and Halving a Square
concepts.description: Constructing a square with double or half the area of a given square, using the diagonal.
concepts.idea: The square built on the diagonal of a given square has exactly double the area; reversing the construction halves the area.
concepts.rule: If a new square is built on the diagonal of a given square, its area is double the original. A square built by folding through the midpoints of the sides (or by reversing the doubling construction) has half the area of the original.
concepts.example: A square of side 4 units has area 16 sq. units; a square built on its diagonal has area 32 sq. units.

concepts.name: The Hypotenuse of an Isosceles Right Triangle
concepts.description: The relationship c squared = 2 times a squared between the equal sides and hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle, derived from the doubling-a-square construction.
concepts.idea: A unit isosceles right triangle's hypotenuse is the side of a square with twice the area of the square on its leg, giving c squared = 2 times a squared.
concepts.rule: For an isosceles right triangle with equal sides a and hypotenuse c, c squared = 2 times a squared. This can be used to find c from a, or a from c.
concepts.example: For a = 12, c squared = 2 x 144 = 288, so c lies between 16 and 17 (since 16 squared = 256 and 17 squared = 289).

concepts.name: The Number the square root of 2
concepts.description: The value of the square root of 2 as the hypotenuse of a unit isosceles right triangle, its decimal bounds, and why it cannot be written as a terminating decimal or a fraction.
concepts.idea: The square root of 2 lies strictly between 1 and 2, and closer bounds such as 1.414 and 1.415 can be found by squaring successive decimals.
concepts.rule: 1 < the square root of 2 < 2, and more precisely 1.414 < the square root of 2 < 1.415. The square root of 2 cannot be written as a terminating decimal, because a terminating decimal squared is also a terminating decimal and never lands exactly on 2. It also cannot be written as a fraction m/n, because that would force the prime 2 to occur an odd number of times on one side of 2 times n squared = m squared and an even number of times on the other, which is impossible.
concepts.example: 1.41 squared = 1.9881 and 1.42 squared = 2.0164, so 1.41 < the square root of 2 < 1.42.

questions.q: In the proof that the square root of 2 is not a fraction, the equation 2 times n squared = m squared leads to a contradiction about how many times the prime 2 appears on each side. questions.a: In m squared, the prime 2 occurs an even number of times (since m squared is a square). In 2 times n squared, the prime 2 occurs an odd number of times (an even number of times from n squared, plus one more from the lone factor of 2). s: States prime 2 occurs an even number of times in m squared

s: Squares 1.4 and 1.5 to bracket the square root of 2 between them

concepts.name: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
concepts.description: Combining two different-sized squares into one larger square using Baudhayana's rectangle-and-diagonal construction, and the resulting theorem relating the three sides of a right triangle.
concepts.idea: Marking a rectangle inside the bigger square using the smaller square's side, and drawing its diagonal, produces four congruent right triangles whose outer figure is itself a square -- showing the sum of the two smaller squares equals the square on the hypotenuse.
concepts.rule: For a right-angled triangle with shorter sides a and b and hypotenuse c, a squared + b squared = c squared. This is the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem, also called the Pythagorean theorem.
concepts.example: For a right triangle with sides 3 and 4, 3 squared + 4 squared = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5 squared, so the hypotenuse is 5.

concepts.name: Baudhayana (Pythagorean) Triples
concepts.description: Sets of three positive integers satisfying a squared + b squared = c squared, including primitive triples, scaled versions, and Fermat's Last Theorem as a related historical fact.
concepts.idea: If (a, b, c) is a Baudhayana triple, then (ka, kb, kc) is also one for any positive integer k; a triple with no common factor greater than 1 is called primitive.
concepts.rule: (a, b, c) is a Baudhayana triple if a squared + b squared = c squared. Scaling every term by the same positive integer k gives another triple. A primitive triple has no common factor greater than 1 among a, b and c. Fermat's Last Theorem states a to the power n + b to the power n = c to the power n has no positive whole-number solution for whole number n greater than 2; it was proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994.
concepts.example: (3, 4, 5) is a primitive Baudhayana triple; (6, 8, 10) is a scaled, non-primitive version of it.

concepts.name: Applying the Pythagoras Theorem
concepts.description: Using a squared + b squared = c squared to solve word problems and geometric problems: diagonals of squares and rectangles, sides of rhombi, checking the longest side of a right triangle, integer-sided rectangles, and the height of an equilateral triangle.
concepts.idea: Once a right triangle can be identified inside a shape or a story problem, the theorem turns a geometry question into an equation to solve.
concepts.rule: In any right triangle, a squared + b squared = c squared, and c (the hypotenuse) is always the longest side. The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and bisect each other, so half of each diagonal and the side form a right triangle. The altitude of an equilateral triangle bisects the base and forms a right triangle with the side and half the base.
concepts.example: A rhombus with diagonals 24 and 70 has half-diagonals 12 and 35, so its side is the square root of (12 squared + 35 squared) = 37 units.
